title: THE MAN THEY STOPPED CALLING JOSEPH
paragraphs:
THE MAN THEY STOPPED CALLING JOSEPH
He Wasn't One of the Twelve. He Didn't Write a Gospel. Yet Without This “Son of Encouragement,” One of Christianity's Greatest Voices Might Have Been Left Standing Outside the Door.
There is something strangely painful about being remembered by your worst chapter.
You know what that feels like.
People remember the mistake.
The divorce.
The addiction.
The season you disappeared from church.
The relationship nobody knows about.
The money you wasted.
The promise you broke.
The years you cannot get back.
The version of yourself you desperately wish people would stop bringing up.
And sometimes the hardest part isn't believing that God can forgive you.
It's wondering whether anyone will ever trust you again.
That is where this story becomes dangerous.
Because buried inside the book of Acts is a man whose ministry repeatedly stood between somebody's past and somebody's future.
His birth name was Joseph.
But eventually, the apostles stopped calling him Joseph.
They called him something else.
Barnabas.
Acts 4:36 preserves the expression in Greek:
υἱὸς παρακλήσεως — huios paraklēseōs.
“Son of encouragement.”
The Greek word παράκλησις — paraklēsis has a richness that a single English word struggles to capture. It can carry the ideas of encouragement, exhortation, appeal, comfort, or strengthening.
So don't imagine Barnabas as merely the pleasant man in church who told everyone to have a nice day.
This was stronger than compliments.
Barnabas had become the kind of man who came alongside people and strengthened them toward faithfulness.
And maybe that is why the apostles' nickname for him became more famous than the name his parents gave him.
Joseph was what he had been called.
Barnabas described what grace had made him.
Think about that.
What would people call you if they named you according to what consistently came out of your life?
Would they call you Son of Encouragement?
Daughter of Mercy?
Bearer of Peace?
Or would the nickname expose something you would rather not see?
Son of Anger.
Daughter of Bitterness.
Carrier of Gossip.
Keeper of Grudges.
Professional Critic.
Christian in public.
Cruel in private.
That question hurts because Christianity was never supposed to be merely something written in our biography.
Following Jesus eventually becomes visible in our behavior.
And Barnabas did not receive his nickname because he posted inspirational sayings.
He received it in the middle of a church where the Gospel was rearranging people's relationship with possessions, status, community, and one another.
Then Luke tells us something almost casually.
Barnabas owned a field.
He sold it.
He brought the proceeds.
He laid them at the apostles' feet.
No spotlight.
No fundraising speech.
No demand that somebody carve his name into a wall.
He simply released something he owned because Christ had taken hold of something deeper.
His heart.
That is where encouragement begins.
Not with words.
With surrender.
Because biblical encouragement costs something.
Sometimes it costs money.
Sometimes time.
Sometimes convenience.
Sometimes reputation.
Sometimes it means standing beside somebody everybody else has already decided is hopeless.
And Barnabas was about to discover exactly how expensive that could become.
Because somewhere else, a man named Saul was building a reputation too.
Only nobody was calling Saul the Son of Encouragement.
Christians were afraid of him.
And they had good reason to be.
Saul had been associated with the violent persecution of believers. Acts places him approvingly at Stephen's death and describes him ravaging the church.
Then Jesus Christ interrupted his road to Damascus.
The persecutor encountered the risen Christ.
The hunter became a disciple.
The enemy became a brother.
But there was a problem.
Jesus knew Saul had changed.
The Christians in Jerusalem weren't so sure.
Can you blame them?
Imagine somebody responsible for terrorizing Christians suddenly arriving at your church saying:
“I'm one of you now.”
Would you hug him?
Or would you wonder whether this was a trap?
Acts 9:26 says Saul tried to join the disciples in Jerusalem, but they were afraid because they did not believe he was really a disciple.
Read that slowly.
Saul had encountered Christ...
and still found himself standing outside human trust.
Maybe you know that place.
Forgiven by God.
Still suspected by people.
Changed...
but surrounded by people who only remember who you used to be.
You repented.
But your family remembers.
You got sober.
But somebody is waiting for you to relapse.
You came back to Jesus.
But people whisper about the years you ran away.
And then Scripture gives us three words that may have altered the course of Christian history:
“But Barnabas took him...”
Barnabas took him.
Everybody else saw danger.
Barnabas saw what Christ was doing.
Everybody else remembered Saul's reputation.
Barnabas listened to Saul's testimony.
Everybody else backed away.
Barnabas stepped closer.
He brought Saul to the apostles and explained what had happened—how Saul had seen the Lord and had boldly preached in the name of Jesus.
Barnabas became a bridge between a redeemed man and a frightened church.
Don't misunderstand this.
Biblical grace is not gullibility.
Christian forgiveness does not mean pretending evil never happened. Wisdom still matters. Accountability matters. Truth matters. Repentance matters.
But Barnabas understood something the church can easily forget:
If Jesus truly transforms someone, we cannot permanently chain that person to the identity Christ has redeemed them from.
Saul's past was real.
So was Christ's grace.
And grace had the final word.
The man once feared as a persecutor would become Paul the missionary, proclaiming Christ across cities and cultures.
Barnabas didn't create Paul's calling.
Jesus did.
Barnabas simply refused to stand in the way of what Jesus was creating.
There is a difference.
And somebody reading this needs to hear it.
You do not need to become somebody's savior.
You already have one.
His name is Jesus Christ.
But you may be called to become somebody's Barnabas.
The person who says:
“I know what you did. But I also see what Christ is doing.”
“I know you failed. But failure doesn't have to become your final identity.”
“I know everyone has given up on you. I haven't.”
“I know your story is messy. Come with me anyway.”
Maybe somebody once did that for you.
Maybe one phone call kept you alive spiritually.
One pastor answered when everybody else was tired of your problems.
One friend sat beside you after your marriage collapsed.
One believer looked past your addiction.
One person invited you back after you disappeared.
One Christian refused to treat your scandal as the end of your story.
You may not remember every sermon you heard during that season.
But you remember who stayed.
That is Barnabas-shaped Christianity.
And his story wasn't finished.
Later, the Gospel began spreading powerfully in Antioch.
When Barnabas arrived and saw the grace of God, Acts tells us that he was glad and encouraged the believers to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose.
Then Scripture gives one of the most beautiful descriptions ever written about a man:
Barnabas was “a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.”
And many people were brought to the Lord.
Notice what Barnabas did next.
He could have enjoyed the growing ministry.
He could have protected his influence.
He could have become the celebrity.
Instead...
he went looking for Saul.
Barnabas traveled to Tarsus to find him.
Let that sink in.
Barnabas saw a growing work of God and thought:
Someone else needs to be here.
That is rare.
We live in a world obsessed with platforms.
Followers.
Recognition.
Credit.
Visibility.
Being quoted.
Being noticed.
Being the person in the photograph.
Barnabas saw a thriving ministry and deliberately brought in someone whose gifts might eventually eclipse his own visibility.
That takes security.
That takes humility.
That takes a man whose identity is rooted somewhere deeper than applause.
It takes somebody who knows that the Kingdom belongs to Jesus.
Not us.
Barnabas found Saul, brought him to Antioch, and together they taught a great many people.
And it was there, at Antioch, that the disciples were first called Christians.
But then comes the part of Barnabas's story that makes him painfully human.
Because encouragement does not mean avoiding conflict.
Paul and Barnabas eventually had one.
A serious one.
A man named John Mark had accompanied them previously but had left them during the mission.
Later Barnabas wanted to take Mark again.
Paul did not.
Paul apparently saw Mark's previous departure as reason not to bring him.
Barnabas saw something worth giving another opportunity.
Acts 15 says the disagreement became sharp.
So sharp that Paul and Barnabas separated.
Paul took Silas.
Barnabas took Mark.
And Scripture does something beautiful here.
It does not turn either man into a cartoon villain.
These were faithful servants of Christ navigating a real disagreement.
But Barnabas did what Barnabas had done before.
He took the man others hesitated to take.
First Saul.
Now Mark.
Do you see the pattern?
Barnabas kept finding people standing dangerously close to being defined by yesterday.
And he kept walking toward them.
He did it for Saul when Saul's problem was a terrible past.
He did it for Mark when Mark's problem was a disappointing failure.
Those are not the same thing.
But Barnabas knew something about restoration.
A person's worst chapter does not necessarily reveal how Jesus intends to finish the book.
And years later...
something remarkable appears in Paul's own writing.
The Paul who once refused to take Mark would eventually tell Timothy:
“Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry.”
Read that again.
Profitable to me for the ministry.
The rejected worker became useful again.
The man who once turned back was wanted again.
The failure wasn't final.
Imagine what might have happened if Mark had been abandoned permanently at his weakest moment.
We cannot know the alternate history.
Scripture does not tell us.
So we should not invent it.
But Scripture does show us that Mark was restored to usefulness—and Barnabas had been willing to walk with him when his reliability was being questioned.
That should terrify some of us.
Because perhaps we have been so busy identifying people's failures that we haven't noticed what Jesus may still be building in them.
Maybe the person you wrote off isn't finished.
Maybe the son who walked away isn't finished.
Maybe the woman whose marriage collapsed isn't finished.
Maybe the pastor who burned out isn't finished.
Maybe the addict fighting through another day isn't finished.
Maybe the teenager questioning everything isn't finished.
Maybe the Christian who disappeared because shame swallowed them isn't finished.
Maybe...
you're not finished.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sin doesn't matter.
Sin matters so much that the Son of God went to a cross.
Jesus did not come to tell us our rebellion was harmless.
He came because we were helpless to save ourselves from it.
At Calvary, Christ bore sin.
Our shame.
Our guilt.
Our condemnation.

The holy Son of God died and rose again so sinners could be reconciled to God—not through religious performance, reputation management, or pretending to be good enough, but through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace walks into darkness and brings sinners into the light.
Repentance does not mean explaining your sin.
It means turning from it toward Christ.
Forgiveness does not mean your past never happened.
It means your past no longer has authority to pronounce the final verdict over someone Jesus has redeemed.
That is why Barnabas matters.
His life points beyond himself.
Toward Christ.
Barnabas encouraged because he had encountered the Gospel of Jesus.
Barnabas gave because Christ had become more valuable than possessions.
Barnabas welcomed because Christ welcomes repentant sinners.
Barnabas restored because Christ restores broken people.
Barnabas could step away from the spotlight because Jesus was the center.
And maybe this article found you because God is putting one uncomfortable question in front of you:
Who needs you to become Barnabas right now?
Not their savior.
Their encourager.
Maybe somebody needs a message tonight.
Not tomorrow.
Tonight.
“I haven't forgotten you.”
Maybe somebody needs you to say:
“Come back to church with me.”
Maybe somebody needs:
“I know you've messed up. But Jesus is still calling you.”
Maybe somebody needs you to stop gossiping about the chapter God is trying to heal.
Maybe the person who needs encouragement lives under your roof.
Your husband.
Your wife.
Your child.
Your father.
Your mother.
Maybe you have been encouraging strangers online while starving your own family of grace.
Or perhaps you are the Saul in this story.
You came to Jesus carrying a history that makes people uncomfortable.
Keep walking with Christ.
Or maybe you're Mark.
You failed.
You left.
You disappointed somebody who trusted you.
And now every time you think about serving God again, a voice whispers:
You had your chance.
Listen carefully.
Your failure may have consequences.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Repentance may require painful honesty.
Restoration may take time.
But none of that means Jesus is finished with you.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Mark turned back.
Paul persecuted believers.
And the church itself is made of people whose only hope is the mercy of Jesus Christ.
There are no trophies of human perfection at the foot of the cross.
Only sinners who needed a Savior.
So come home.
Stop negotiating with the sin Jesus is telling you to surrender.
Stop protecting what is killing your fellowship with God.
Stop pretending.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Be honest.
And if Christ has already restored you from something you thought would destroy your life, tell somebody what Jesus did. Your testimony may become another person's Barnabas moment.
Then think of one specific person who needs this message.
Not your entire friends list.
One person.
You already know their name.
Send this to the believer who thinks failure disqualified them forever.
If Christ has given you truth that can point another wounded person toward Him, don't bury it.
Because eventually you may become the person who needs to read it again.
Supporting Gospel work does not purchase God's favor. It does not earn salvation. It does not make anyone more spiritual.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But believers who have freely received can freely choose to help Gospel-centered ministry reach others.
And whether you ever spend a cent or not, keep pursuing Christ.
Because Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
Barnabas's story leaves us with something we desperately need in an age that enjoys public humiliation.
The world knows how to expose people.
Jesus knows how to redeem them.
The world knows how to screenshot your worst moment.
Jesus knows how to write your next chapter.
The world says:
“Remember what they did.”
Grace says:
“Look what Christ is doing.”
Barnabas was born Joseph.
But grace shaped his life so deeply that people eventually knew him by what flowed through him.
Encouragement.
Perhaps that is the question you should carry after closing this article.
Not:
“Will people remember my name?”
But:
“When people remember how I treated them at their lowest, will they remember something that looked like Jesus?”
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is standing outside a door.
Somebody is ashamed.
Somebody failed.
Somebody believes their usefulness to God ended in their worst chapter.
And perhaps God is not asking you to preach them a sermon.
Perhaps He is simply asking you to walk toward them...
take them by the hand...
and remind them that Jesus Christ is still writing.
Never confuse the chapter where someone fell with the chapter where Jesus intends to finish their story.
